taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes S. uniformis was elevated to a full species (Schulte et al. 2006), returned to synonymy with S. magister (Leache and Mulcahy 2007), and is currently recognized as a full species by Crother (2017); Wikipedia says it was a subspecies of S. magister until recently.
fieldMarks: Large, robust spiny lizard: adults to about 5.5 in (14 cm) snout-to-vent, tail slightly longer than the body.
Brown or tan with yellow and black dorsal stripes or mottling and a black collar on each side of the neck.
Males are larger, with a swollen tail base, enlarged postanal scales and femoral pores, and bluish markings on the throat and belly.
Females have a pale throat and belly with faint or no blue; a female's head may turn orange or reddish in the breeding season.
behavior: Mainly an ambush predator that sometimes forages actively; eats ants, beetles, grasshoppers, spiders, centipedes and caterpillars, and occasionally small lizards, nestling birds and plant material.
Basks in the morning on rocks or other sunlit hard surfaces and shelters, usually underground, during the hottest part of a summer day.
Hibernates from late fall through winter and emerges in spring.
Uses trees, rocks and the ground near cover; eggs are laid in soil.
habitat: Arid and semiarid country from plains to lower mountain slopes: desert shrubland and woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, juniper and mesquite woodland, shrubby arroyos and cottonwood-willow along rivers.
range: California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah (Mojave, Great Basin and San Joaquin deserts); endemic to the United States, not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Desert spiny lizard (Sceloporus magister)
lookalikes.howToTell: Treated as a subspecies of S. magister until recently; the sources read give no field character, so separate mainly by range and the black neck collar with yellow dorsal pattern described here.
